newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's second city tilts to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's second city tilts to rebels.

text.p: Zaire's second city prepared on Monday to greet the advancing forces of rebel leader Laurent Kabila, driving another nail into the coffin of President Mobutu Sese Seko's tottering regime.
Residents of Lubumbashi woke up to surprise news that the rebels were approaching in force from the southwest, where they had taken control of the town of Kipushi on the Zambian border before dawn.

Shops and businesses were closed and the streets emptied, but groups of cheering onlookers later formed outside one army barracks in the city where government troops tied on white headbands to signal their switch to Kabila.
"We've all changed sides. We're ready for the arrival of Kabila," said Sergeant Kafua Otamba of the 21st Brigade, who spoke to Reuters at the Lido barracks, one of many in Lubumbashi.
Inside, dozens of soldiers sported new white headbands, but it was not clear whether the army had gone over wholesale to the rebels, or what the elite presidential guard intended to do.
"We've suffered enough in Zaire over the last 30 years. We must get rid of Mobutu. We've had no pay and we have no food," Otamba said.

Cheering townspeople crowded around soldiers manning a roadblock outside the barracks. Apollinaire Kasongo, a teacher, said: "We have suffered with these soldiers. We are very proud of them (deciding to change sides)."

In South Africa, peace talks resumed on Monday between Kabila representatives and government envoys. But in a further sign that the tide may be turning against Mobutu, diamond-mining giant De Beers, the firm which controls the world's diamond market, said it had held weekend talks with Kabila.

De Beers has trading offices in Zaire's diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi, which was taken by Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) on Saturday as the peace talks began in Pretoria.

After weeks of tense speculation, Lubumbashi's fate appeared sealed when a force of at least several hundred rebel troops swept through Kipushi just 30 km (20 miles) away and advanced along the road towards the copperbelt capital itself.
Lubumbashi was effectively encircled, leaving no clear avenue of escape for government troops and the elite presidential guard units recently sent to reinforce them.

The headquarters of the Gecamines mining company decided to shut up shop, pushing up cobalt prices in European trading. Sizarail, a Belgian-South African consortium which runs local railways, also packed away its communications equipment.
Zaire airlines cancelled all flights to Lubumbashi and a scheduled flight from Johannesburg was cancelled.
Local radio broadcast appeals, apparently from members of the army, calling on fellow soldiers to greet the rebels as brothers and refrain from looting.
In what was widely seen as a coded message that there should be no armed resistance, the governor of mineral-rich Shaba province Kyungu wa Kumwanza urged that all bloodshed be avoided.
Surprised residents in Kipushi, which lies hard by the Zambian border to the southwest of Lubumbashi, said by telephone the rebel force had entered the town from the direction of the southern border.
"There were perhaps one to two thousand, all armed and in uniform and mostly young," said local businessman Gilbert Mbangu. They met no resistance and walked on to Lubumbashi at dawn.
Government troops had melted away and there had been no violence or looting in Kipushi, Mbangu said.
